objectives: Explain who Ahmed Yesevî was.
Explain the words pîr, order and hikmet.
Say what his poems and the Yesevî Path aimed to do.
Use known as, means and aimed to.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter is full of definitions. A definition chart (word → meaning → example) helps learners handle pîr, order and hikmet, and shows how writers explain words inside a text.
anticipatedMisconceptions: ‘Order’ here means a spiritual path, not a command.
He wrote and recited his poems in plain Turkish, not in Persian.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: known as (extra information) · means · be called · aimed to + verb
Notice (Activity 1): Ahmed Yesevî, known as Pîr-i Turkistan, …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *known like · *the word mean · *aimed spreading.
Use (Activity 4): a person with a title.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ah-MED ye-se-VÎ, PÎR-i tur-kis-TAN, hik-MET.
Stress: re-CITE, SPIR-it-u-al, FOUND-er.

duringReading: First reading: Who was Ahmed Yesevî?

Find what his poems aimed to do.

objectives: Describe Yesevî’s childhood and education.
Explain the old and modern names of Yesi.
Explain what Turkestan was like in his time.
Use It is believed that and which is now.

anticipatedMisconceptions: He was born in Sayram and moved to Yesi; he was not born in Yesi.
The Karakhanid dates (840–1212) are the dates of the state, not of Yesevî’s life.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: It is believed that · which is now · grow up · at a time when
Notice (Activity 1): It is believed that he was born …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then correct errors.
Likely errors: *It believed that · *various field.
Use (Activity 4): a place then and now.

Find what Turkestan was like.

content.teacherReflection: Did learners separate facts from beliefs?

content.chapter: Chapter 3: Master and Return to Yesi
objectives: Describe Yesevî’s years in Bukhara in order.
Explain the role of Sheikh Yûsuf el-Hemedânî.
Explain what Yesevî did after his master died.
Use who clauses, after, when and then.
content.pedagogy: A chain of teachers and students: Arslan Baba, Hemedânî, Yesevî and Gucdüvânî. A simple chain diagram helps learners keep the names and see how knowledge passed from person to person.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Yesevî handed over his duty to Gucdüvânî; Gucdüvânî was not his teacher.
He returned to Yesi at the end and died there in 1166.
content.grammarFocus:

Notice (Activity 1): a famous Sufi master who played the greatest role …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the time words, then rewrite.

Use (Activity 4): a teacher who trained me.

content.teacherReflection: Did learners follow the chain of teachers?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “after” and one with “who” about Yesevî.

Explain why people loved him.
Describe the nomadic communities near the Syr Darya River.
Use because and because of.
content.pedagogy: A very short chapter with one key reason. The contrast between “because” and “because of” is clear in the text, so it is a good moment to focus on it.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Nomadic communities moved from place to place; they did not live in one city.
People loved him for his language and wisdom, not for power.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: because of + noun phrase · because + clause · so
Notice (Activity 1): because of his simple language …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *because of he used · *because his simple language.
Use (Activity 4): a speaker people love.

duringReading: First reading: Where did Yesevî become widely known?

Find the river.

content.transferTask: Write about a person whose words people love.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use because and because of correctly?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “because of” and one with “because”.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: The Yesevî Path and the Mausoleum
objectives: Explain how the Yesevî Path spread.
Describe the history of the mausoleum from Timur to TİKA.
Explain why people wanted to be buried near it.
Use the past passive and the present perfect passive.
content.pedagogy: A long chapter with dates and a building story. A timeline (1166 → 1389–1405 → 1405 → 2003 → today) organizes the facts, and the passive appears naturally because the building is the topic.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Timur ordered the mausoleum, but it was left unfinished when he died.
TİKA completed the restoration and landscaping; it did not build the mausoleum.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: was + past participle · have been + past participle · order something to be built · to be buried
Notice (Activity 1): the construction was left unfinished.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then correct errors.

Use (Activity 4): a historic building I know.

content.transferTask: Write about a historic building you know.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use the timeline to order the facts?

exitTicket: Write one passive sentence about the mausoleum.

objectives: Explain why Yesevî chose Turkish.
Describe his education and his goals.
Explain how his teachings spread.
Use However, which (whole idea) and Thanks to.
content.pedagogy: The chapter explains a language choice and its effect on identity. A three-column chart (Arabic / Persian / Turkish) shows the roles of the languages, and learners connect the choice of language with the aim of reaching ordinary people.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Yesevî knew the scholarly languages well; he chose Turkish on purpose.
He sent the scholars he trained to the Turkmen tribes; he did not travel to all of them himself.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: which (referring to a whole idea) · However · Thanks to + noun · in a way that
Notice (Activity 1): …, which helped develop a Turkish identity.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the linkers, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *Thanks to his followers spread · *However he chose (no comma).
Use (Activity 4): why my language matters.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ha-NA-fi, MAD-ra-sa, sha-REE-a, dî-VÂN-ı hik-MET.
Stress: i-DEN-ti-ty, LIT-er-a-ture, in-tro-DUCE.

duringReading: First reading: Why did Yesevî choose Turkish?
Second reading: complete the three-language chart.
Find his main goal.

How can a language help build an identity?
Why did he use simple and clear teachings?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Arabic and Persian” and “Dîvân-ı Hikmet” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: strict, introduce, the universe.

differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short speech by Yesevî explaining why he writes in Turkish.

expectedResponses: People used Arabic for religion and Persian for literature. However, Yesevî wrote in Turkish, which helped develop a Turkish identity. Thanks to his followers, his path spread to many places.

content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect the language choice with identity?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “However” and one with “Thanks to”.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: The Path of Wisdom and Society
objectives: Explain the main goal of wisdom for Yesevî.
List the bad feelings and good values in the chapter.
Describe the social problems in his poems.
Use must, not only … but also and even if.
content.pedagogy: The chapter moves from inner life (ego, greed, patience) to society (orphans, strangers, cruel rulers). A two-part chart (inner life / society) helps learners see that, for Yesevî, wisdom is about both.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “True wisdom means being a good and real human being” is a summary of his view, not a religious rule.
He criticized dishonest judges and cruel rulers, not all judges and rulers.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: must + base verb · not only … but also · even if · those who
Notice (Activity 1): did not only focus on … but also wrote …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then correct errors.
Likely errors: *must to develop · *Education and self-discipline is.
Use (Activity 4): being a good person today.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: hu-MIL-i-ty, PA-tience, OR-phans, op-PRESSED.
Linking: “not only” /nɒt ˈoʊnli/.
beforeReading: Ask: “What makes a person truly good?”
duringReading: First reading: What is the main goal of wisdom?
Second reading: complete the chart: inner life / society.
Find whom he criticized.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: being a good person; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does it mean to leave the ego behind?
Why does Yesevî say religion is not just about sin and reward?
Which social problems from his poems still exist today?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Good Values” and “Social Problems” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: behind, sin, reward.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with “greed” and “orphans” written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short poem of four lines with Yesevî’s advice in modern English.

formativeAssessment: Uses not only … but also correctly.
expectedResponses: For Yesevî, the main goal of wisdom is to leave the ego behind. He not only wrote about religious topics but also about social problems, such as caring for orphans and strangers.
content.transferTask: Write about what a good person must do today.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect inner values with social action?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “not only … but also”.

objectives: Explain Yesevî’s education method.
Explain why love is necessary in teaching.
Describe how his movement spread.
Use only possible if, so that and even if.
content.pedagogy: A chapter about teaching that speaks directly to classrooms today. Learners can compare Yesevî’s method with their own experience and discuss what helps them learn.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Love here means love for what students learn and kindness from the teacher, not only friendship.
“Even if they learn it” means learning without love does not lead to acceptance.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: only possible if · even if · so that · For this reason
Notice (Activity 1): only possible if you make them love what they learn.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *so that students listen to (missing will / can) · *even they learn.
Use (Activity 4): how the best teachers teach.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: PROP-er-ly, KIND-ness, MOVE-ment, DIS-tant.
Intonation: “even IF they learn it”.
beforeReading: Ask: “Which lesson do you love? Why?”
duringReading: First reading: What was his method centered on?
Second reading: underline the condition and the purpose.
Find how far his poems reached.

discussionPoints: Why will people not accept something they do not love?
Do you agree with Yesevî’s method? Why?

interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Love in Teaching” and “Distant Tribes” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames: Teaching is only possible if … / so that students …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short letter from a student to a teacher who made them love a subject.

content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect the method with their own learning?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “so that” about teaching.

objectives: Name the three works believed to belong to Yesevî.
Explain why the texts were probably written down later.
Explain why the Dîvân-ı Hikmet is important.
Use are believed to, the passive with by and probably.
content.pedagogy: The chapter shows careful historical writing: the works are “believed to belong” to Yesevî and were “probably” written down later. Learners notice how writers show what is certain and what is not.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The texts we have today were written down later; this does not mean that the ideas are not his.
The Dîvân-ı Hikmet is a collection of many hikmets, not one long poem.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: be believed to + verb · passive with by · himself (emphasis) · probably · pass down
Notice (Activity 1): are believed to belong to Ahmed Yesevî.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then correct errors.
Likely errors: *are believe to · *were not wrote.
Use (Activity 4): a saying passed down in my family.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: fakr-NÂ-me, ri-SÂ-le der a-DÂB-i ta-RÎ-kat.
Stress: gen-er-A-tions, LIT-er-a-ture, CO-llec-tion.
beforeReading: Ask: “Do you know a saying that your grandparents often use?”
duringReading: First reading: Which works belong to Yesevî?

Find why hikmets are important.

expectedResponses: Three works are believed to belong to Yesevî. The texts we have today were not written by him; people passed his sayings down and probably wrote them down much later.
content.transferTask: Write about a saying passed down in your family.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners notice how the writer shows certainty?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “is / are believed to”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains how the texts reached us.

objectives: Explain the two ways the Qur’an looks at wisdom.
Explain Maqasid al-Sharia and the five things it protects.
Explain the difference between rules and wisdom.
Use While (contrast), Without and so that.
content.pedagogy: A long idea chapter. A three-part map helps: (1) wisdom in the Qur’an (an aim of education, a gift from Allah), (2) the goals of Islamic law (five things), (3) rules and wisdom (what/how versus why). Keep the discussion within the book’s wording.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “While” here compares; it does not mean “at the same time”.
“To prevent” is the original meaning of the Arabic word; wisdom prevents ignorance and injustice.

Targets: While (contrast) · Without + noun · so that · come from
Notice (Activity 1): While law answers “What?” and “How?”, wisdom answers “Why?”.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *Without wisdom rules has · *so that people lives.
Use (Activity 4): the wisdom behind a rule.

duringReading: First reading: What are the two ways the Qur’an looks at wisdom?

interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Maqasid al-Sharia” and “Five Important Things” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the three-part map with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph comparing rules and wisdom with While and Without.

formativeAssessment: Explains the two views of wisdom.
expectedResponses: The Qur’an shows wisdom as an aim of education and as a gift from Allah. While law answers “What?” and “How?”, wisdom answers “Why?”. Without wisdom, rules have no meaning.
content.transferTask: Write about the wisdom behind a rule.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners explain the difference between rules and wisdom?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “While” that compares two things.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the two views of wisdom.

content.chapter: Chapter 11: Wisdom in the Qur’an and Hadith
objectives: Explain why every action should have a purpose.
Explain what the verses in the chapter say about wisdom.
Explain what the hadith about the lost treasure teaches.

Use who clauses, turn … into and still.

metadata.title: Ahmed Yesevî B1 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Pîr-i Turkistan
metadata.estimatedDuration: 13 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow connected texts about history, ideas and values, and who can produce supported explanations and short reflections.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through Ahmed Yesevî: his life and teachers, the Yesevî Path and the mausoleum, his choice of Turkish, his ideas about wisdom and teaching, the Dîvân-ı Hikmet and its lines, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 13 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a map, a date or a picture.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: definitions, a timeline, a building story, ideas with reasons, quotations with sources or poem lines.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practice it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: known as (extra information) · means · be called · aimed to + verb
Ch2: It is believed that · which is now · grow up · at a time when
Ch3: who (defining) · after / when + past · then · hand over
Ch4: because of + noun phrase · because + clause · so
Ch5: was + past participle · have been + past participle · order something to be built · to be buried
Ch6: which (referring to a whole idea) · However · Thanks to + noun · in a way that
Ch7: must + base verb · not only … but also · even if · those who
Ch8: only possible if · even if · so that · For this reason
Ch9: be believed to + verb · passive with by · himself (emphasis) · probably · pass down
Ch10: While (contrast) · Without + noun · so that · come from
Ch11: so … either · In fact · It does not matter who / where · invite someone to + verb
Ch12: who (defining) · turn … into · still · be like + noun
Ch13: It would be better for … to + verb · if (first conditional) · even if · having + past participle

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, people, places and key ideas.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify main ideas, timelines, reasons, contrasts and the writer’s certainty.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: describe people and places, explain ideas and give reasons.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce connected B1 paragraphs using evidence, linking words and chapter patterns.

valuesFocus: D14 Respect — Respect for teachers, elders and all people.
D20 Helpfulness — Caring for people in need.
D16 Responsibility — Teaching with care and love.
languageFocus: Every one of the 13 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the thinking target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, picture cards, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for one more sentence or one more reason from the book, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.

Chapter 11 quotes verses of the Qur’an and a hadith with their sources; Chapter 13 gives lines from the Dîvân that mention verses and the sayings of the Prophet. These belong to the teacher-approved text; they are read as they are, without extra comment, and the exercises do not change their words.
Chapter 10 explains religious ideas such as haram, helal and Maqasid al-Sharia in the words of the book; keep the discussion within these words.
Chapter 9 says that the works are “believed to belong” to Yesevî and were “probably” written down later; present these as the writer’s careful explanations.
Bracketed Turkish words and the Turkish poem lines belong to the teacher-approved story; they are read as they are.

metadata.title: Ahmed Yesevî B1 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 25 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B1 learners who study Ahmed Yesevî alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 13 chapters of Ahmed Yesevî.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Follow the life, teachers and heritage of Ahmed Yesevî.
Explain his ideas about language, wisdom and teaching with evidence from the book.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 13.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One idea of Ahmed Yesevî that I would like to remember:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 13 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 25 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows respect, helpfulness, responsibility and diligence. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Respect: Respect: Turkic peoples still respect Yesevî, and he asked people not to hurt anyone, even non-believers (Chapters 5, 7 and 13).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: Yesevî wrote about caring for orphans and strangers and helping oppressed people (Chapter 7).
Responsibility: Responsibility: Teachers must treat their students with love and kindness so that they focus on the lessons (Chapter 8).
Diligence: Diligence: Yesevî studied with great teachers in Yesi and Bukhara, and education and self-discipline are very important on the path of wisdom (Chapters 3 and 7).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 13, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell someone at home in five sentences who Ahmed Yesevî was and why he chose Turkish, in your home language or in English.
